arxiv:2611.21072.text: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report. From Kun Cai and colleagues. Scientific models need to handle more than text: they must interpret biological data, use tools, and complete tasks that can be checked. Sage S1.5 Flash combines special encoders for molecular graphs, biological sequences, and spectra with a shared model, and it trains agent skills in environments where results can be verified. Across thirty-three benchmarks, it ranked first in four named comparisons, including tests of documentary evidence, spreadsheets, and machine learning tasks. It also performed competitively on desktop and browser tasks guided by visual feedback.

arxiv:2611.21218.text: InclusionMed: Benchmarking AI for Inclusive Healthcare. From The InclusionMed Collaboration. Medical AI benchmarks cover healthcare roles, tasks, and settings unevenly, making it hard to judge how well models serve diverse needs. InclusionMed brings benchmarks together in an Atlas, selecting four public benchmarks from three hundred eighty-eight candidates and adding a private diagnostic reasoning benchmark. Across the five benchmarks, frontier models scored from seventeen point five to forty-nine point one out of one hundred, and their rankings changed depending on the role or capability assessed. The ten highest-ranked models did better on patient communication than on clinical decision-making, underscoring the need to choose models for specific care needs.

arxiv:2611.19937.text: AllocFlow: End-to-End Portfolio Trading Action Generation from Raw Market Data. From Annan Wang and colleagues. Portfolio systems often forecast each asset separately, which can leave those forecasts misaligned with the final allocation. AllocFlow instead learns to generate coordinated positions across assets directly from market histories, first imitating a trading strategy and then refining decisions with reinforcement learning using portfolio-level rewards. On hourly cryptocurrency futures, refinement raised annualized net return from twenty-seven point seven nine percent to fifty-one point three eight percent, and the Calmar ratio from zero point nine five five to four point zero four three. On six further months of unseen data, it reached a Calmar ratio of four point nine without retraining.

arxiv:2611.20218.text: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations. From Xinping Lei and colleagues. Software teams must turn incomplete requests into working changes by finding requirements, coordinating with colleagues, and checking the result. SWE-CoWork tests this in 101 assignments drawn from real software repositories, with simulated coworkers and private tests. The best models pass about 63 percent of tests for changes they begin, but finish fewer than eight percent of assignments. Even when given complete requirements upfront, they do not finish more tasks, pointing to a need for better follow-through from clarification to verification and handoff.

arxiv:2611.20254.text: VoxMel TTS Technical Report. From Wenhao Guan and colleagues. Autoregressive speech synthesis needs a sound representation that is easy to predict without losing detail. VoxMel avoids a learned encoder by splitting mel spectrograms into coarse speech features and two layers of finer detail, using a reversible transform. The system predicts the coarse features one step at a time, then fills in the details separately. On English and Chinese tests, it achieves low word and character error rates, and a four-step version nearly matches the supervised model's accuracy while retaining competitive speaker similarity.

arxiv:2611.20986.text: Calpha: Toward Native Biomolecular Intelligence in a General-Purpose Language Model. From Yong Liu and colleagues. Protein structure prediction and language reasoning have largely remained separate, limiting how much each can contribute to the other. Calpha connects a language model to a pretrained structure-prediction tool: it reads protein sequences enriched with features from Evolutionary Scale Modeling two, then passes its internal representations to the tool to predict a single-chain structure. The system achieved mean Template Modeling scores of 0.808 on FoldBench-334, 0.635 on CASP16 domains, and 0.900 on a CAMEO-style set. Its current comparisons show lower scores for longer chains, while protein training also reduced accuracy on the tested language-reasoning questions.

arxiv:2611.21003.text: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models. From K2 Team and colleagues. K2-Horizon tackles the need for open language models that can reason and handle practical tasks, from coding to office work. It releases six models and the data, training records, code, and data-building pipelines needed to study how they were made. The team also introduces new attention methods and a way to speed up decoding without a separate draft model. One smaller model nearly matches a similarly trained dense model while using one-seventh as many active parameters, and decoding can be up to two point two times faster.

arxiv:2611.21607.text: ScaleVLA: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models to 552 Billion Parameters. From Ruixi Yu and colleagues. Robot policies often use much smaller vision-language models than those now capable of controlling robots, leaving their learned knowledge underused. ScaleVLA connects a five hundred and fifty-two-billion-parameter model to a trainable action module, then compares it with smaller models under the same training setup. With just ten demonstrations, it beats a smaller model trained on fifty, and it achieves higher success on new tasks and precise charger insertion. Each action chunk takes a median of two hundred and sixteen milliseconds.

arxiv:2611.20882.text: Accelerate Bench: Evaluating Agents for Application-Level Program Optimization. From Bowen Liu and colleagues. Optimizing a complete application means finding useful code changes while preserving the required computation, and it can be hard to tell whether coding agents succeed. Accelerate Bench tests agents on thirty-two CPU optimization tasks adapted from scientific applications and supercomputing competitions, with clear rules for correctness, timing, and permitted edits. Across sixteen agents, Score at One ranges from 25.5 percent to 67.4 percent, and the two leading agents achieve at least double the speed on twenty-two or more tasks. The results also show that build and runtime choices, and how changes work together, can strongly affect performance.

arxiv:2611.21339.text: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos. From Yunyang Ge and colleagues. Long-form video generators often lose quality beyond their training length, while their growing memory costs make streaming harder. MovieRoll combines methods for training on video chunks, compressing stored history, and extending generation beyond the training horizon. Its cache compression cuts memory use by up to seventy-eight percent while improving quality, and its distilled version earns the highest overall scores among compared methods on evaluations up to sixty seconds. This suggests the system can sustain natural-looking video with active motion over longer durations.

arxiv:2611.20404.text: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier. From Benhao Huang and colleagues. When high-quality training data runs out, repeating it helps less with each pass. This study tests whether latent feedback, which passes each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, uses the same compute better than a standard Transformer trained for more epochs. Across model sizes and data amounts, it generally improves how much each unit of compute and data is worth, except when unique data is scarce for the model size. At most, it saves forty-eight percent of compute and forty-seven percent of unique data, making it a stronger use of compute when data is the bottleneck.

arxiv:2611.21479.text: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control. From Shaohao Rui and colleagues. Hand-controlled video worlds need to respond accurately to movements while generating scenes quickly enough for real-time use. LynnReal-Hand combines a collection of one hundred thousand interaction clips with training methods for detailed hand and object motion, fast video generation, and a compact decoder. On HandBench, it outperforms existing methods in hand-following accuracy and visual quality. Its three-step model keeps a high hand accuracy score, and its streaming system reaches eighteen frames per second at five hundred and forty p resolution.

arxiv:2611.21439.text: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space. From Jacky Kumar. Finding plausible new physics explanations is difficult because many Standard Model Effective Field Theory operators can affect different measurements at once. This work treats the search as a sequence of choices, using a small reinforcement learning agent to build theories from combinations of operators. Tested on 132 measurements, the agent found diverse multi-operator theories that substantially improved the overall fit. Compared with two random search methods, it navigated the large set of possibilities more effectively.

arxiv:2611.19771.text: JEPA4R: Embodied JEPA World Models with 4D Point Planning. From Jiarui Dong and colleagues. Robot world models need to represent the geometry of objects, not just how scenes look, and it can be hard to see what they imagine. JEPA4R uses point clouds from a depth camera to predict future scenes in a compact space, plan movements, and guide a robot policy. Its decoded predictions stay within one point one centimeters of the target on average over two hundred steps, and it leads on several benchmark tasks. Policies trained only in a digital twin also work on a real robot arm without extra training.

arxiv:2611.20192.text: GlyphAtlas: Disentangling Stroke Detail from Layout for Scene Text Synthesis. From Luozheng Qin and colleagues. Scene text generators can struggle to render fine strokes when characters are small, tightly packed, or complex, because glyph detail is tied to the size of its target region. GlyphAtlas keeps a layout image as a spatial guide and adds a separate atlas with high-resolution references for each character or word. Its attention mechanism links each text region to the matching atlas cells, refining stroke detail while preserving layout. Experiments show accurate rendering of challenging text, transfer to languages unseen during task-specific training, and leading performance in scenes with many text regions.

arxiv:2611.20148.text: Centered Ablation: Why Last-Layer Directional Ablation Under-Fires or Collapses, and a Closed-Form Fix. From Quy-Anh Dang and colleagues. Directional ablation is meant to switch off a model behavior, but it can miss its target or make the model repeat itself. The work shows that, in the final layer, ablation acts like a vocabulary-wide bias whose strength depends on how the hidden state aligns with the behavior direction. Centered Ablation removes the shared component in that direction, improving attack success by 29 to 46 points on models where standard ablation underperforms and reducing repetition collapse on Gemma-2-9B from 50 percent to 1 percent. It also preserves more benign answers, while showing that safety judges can score collapsed text in opposing ways.

arxiv:2611.20385.text: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images. From Emilio Ferrara. Predicting a chain reaction from a still image requires working out which small physical differences decide what happens. DominoBench tests this with 854 simulated scenes, arranged in pairs where a tiny change can flip whether a person survives. Across 30 vision-language models, even leading systems got the deciding person right on no more than 72 percent of scenes, and got both scenes in a pair right on no more than 34 percent. Giving them the key calculation raised their accuracy to 82 to 92 percent, showing that they can use the answer but usually cannot work it out themselves.

arxiv:2611.19537.text: Continuation-Guided LLM Evolution of Program Policies and Goal Compilers in Craftax. From Víctor Gallego. Long-horizon game policies can improve on local feedback yet still fail at the final goal, while adapting them to a new goal can require another costly round of code generation. In Craftax, the framework refines policies through a cascade of feedback, from episode scores to hierarchical goals and belief updates. This raises arrival at the final stage from less than one percent to fifty percent, with final boss defeats in twenty-eight percent of runs. A reusable goal compiler also transfers from short tasks to longer ones without task-specific tuning or calls to a language model during play.

arxiv:2611.19649.text: LoopFill: Pipelined Multi-Token Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers. From Siqi Zhu and colleagues. Looped Transformers reuse the same layers, which saves parameters but makes each generated token take several sequential passes. LoopFill combines shallow predictions with multi-token suffix drafts in one shared draft tree, allowing several future tokens to enter the pipeline together. It then checks candidates at different loop depths in a batch, while full-depth verification preserves the model's output distribution. Across seven benchmarks, it averages five point eight five times the greedy decoding speed on Ouro and five point one three times on Huginn, beating the strongest baseline.

arxiv:2611.21599.text: Hyperlyve: Parallelized Enumeration and Exact Lyapunov Stability Certification for Deep ReLU Networks. From Brian Yarbrough and colleagues. Certifying stability in nonlinear systems controlled by deep neural networks can be computationally difficult. Hyperlyve learns and formally checks piecewise-affine neural Lyapunov functions, using a parallel method to split the system into regions defined by ReLU activations and test stability conditions in each one. Its tests certify the exact smooth dynamics within a compact domain, and the work shows that this verification problem is co-NP-complete. In experiments, Hyperlyve enumerated ReLU networks more than one hundred and fifty times faster than competing tools, enabling proofs for systems beyond current verifiers.

arxiv:2611.20336.text: Spectral Landmarks: Alignment of Landmark Kernel Translates with the Leading Eigenfunctions of a Kernel Operator. From Jeanie Schreiber. Choosing landmark points well can help kernel methods capture the most important patterns in their data. This work defines a measure of how closely the landmark functions span the leading eigenfunctions, and connects it to a standard measure of approximation error. It shows that the best landmarks balance how the eigenfunctions are sampled, with especially precise characterizations on symmetric spaces. In tests, optimization from random starts found evenly spaced points on a circle and regular polyhedra on a sphere.

arxiv:2611.21547.text: Fundamental Tradeoffs in Sampling, Transmission and Information Freshness: Instantaneous Feedback. From Subhankar Banerjee and colleagues. The work studies how to keep status updates fresh when sending them can fail and both sampling and transmission rates are limited. It derives lower bounds and analyzes policies that choose when to wait, retransmit an old update, or replace it with a fresh one. In the intermediate range of rate limits, it reduces the search to mixtures of these policies and shows that a mixture of four achieves age within a factor of two of optimal. This gives a practical way to balance update freshness against limited resources.

arxiv:2611.20179.text: Radar Waveform Design via Convex Semidefinite Relaxation. From Samuel Pinilla. Radar waveforms are often designed to have a desired ambiguity function, which describes how well they distinguish targets by range and Doppler. Existing methods for the narrowband case can get trapped short of the best solution, making recovery depend on the starting point. The wavex method lifts waveform recovery into a convex optimization problem and uses relaxed reflections, semidefinite steps, and a final local refinement. In numerical tests, it accurately recovered band-limited pulses from complete or heavily reduced ambiguity data when enough samples remained, and handled increasing noise with gradually lower accuracy.

arxiv:2611.21286.text: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches. From Michael Wieck-Sosa and colleagues. High-dimensional data can make neural posterior estimation costly, while hand-designed summaries take substantial effort to build. This work instead estimates the parameter's posterior from a small set of low-dimensional random sketches of the data. It shows that, for a model with a parameter of dimension p, two p plus one sketches are enough for posterior consistency. In comparisons, the approach matches the best embedding network and uses computation more efficiently.

arxiv:2611.21480.text: RESILAGENT: A Three-Pillar Architecture for Cyber-Physical Resilience in Electrical Power and Energy Systems. From Nikolaos Kekatos and colleagues. Power and energy systems face threats that mix cyberattacks, physical sabotage, and climate stress, while monitoring tools often work in separate silos. RESILAGENT proposes three connected pillars for sensing, resilience analysis, and incident response, coordinated through a cloud system and a cycle of detection, simulation, decision, and signing. It combines artificial intelligence, digital twins, and a permissioned blockchain, and is tested on two threat scenarios. An IEEE-bus benchmark measures the pillars' performance, though the abstract gives no results.

arxiv:2611.21542.text: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction. From Yu Gui and colleagues. Online conformal prediction must balance reliable long-run coverage under changing or adversarial data against stable coverage when data are independent and identically distributed. This work studies how that balance depends on how tightly long-run coverage is required to match its target. It proves a phase transition: for deviations shrinking no faster than the square-root rate, algorithms can retain split conformal's instantaneous coverage performance on independent data while guaranteeing long-run coverage against adversarial data. Tighter requirements come at a cost.

arxiv:2611.21362.text: What You Post Is What You Symptom: Estimating Psychometric Networks from Social Media Discourse. From Ştefana-Arina Tăbuşcă and colleagues. Symptom networks usually rely on questionnaires, which limit analysis to the symptoms they include. This work estimates symptom networks from social media posts about depression and eating disorders, and checks patterns in a separate anorexia group. For depression, post-based scores tracked questionnaire totals, and nearly all questionnaire items showed a significant link. Most network connections were similar across posts and questionnaires, though bridge symptoms differed. Linguistic features also showed the same direction across all three groups.

arxiv:2611.20256.text: Continuous-Time Stochastic Contraction Induced by Common White Noise. From Sunghyun Koo and colleagues. Stochastic systems can move apart or draw together, even when two trajectories experience the same random input. This work develops tests for when their separation shrinks, using distances that cover both familiar geometric and norm-based measures. It gives necessary and sufficient differential conditions for exponential contraction in average moments and along almost every path. The theory also links contraction to input-to-state stability and shows how noise can synchronize systems, while measuring robustness to parameter changes.

arxiv:2611.20131.text: Quadrature-Induced Local Minima in Structure-Preserving Lotka-Volterra Control. From Alexandre Autran. Harvest accounting can alter an optimal control problem even when its population model stays unchanged. For a positivity-preserving predator–prey scheme, the study compares rewarding the actual removal of prey with estimating harvest from the prey count at the start of each time step. That estimate can make the cost curve bend down and create a strict local minimum that is not the best solution. With diffusion, the two approaches differ by an amount that shrinks in proportion to the time step, uniformly across spatial grids.

arxiv:2611.21395.text: The Sample Complexity of Channel Coding. From Terence Viaud and colleagues. This work asks how long a message must be sent through a noisy channel to meet a target error rate and transmission rate. It develops a nonasymptotic way to measure that required blocklength, and derives explicit bounds for discrete memoryless channels. The key finding is that this length is governed not by the usual channel capacity, but by a different measure of channel performance called the order-one-half Augustin–Csiszár capacity. The work also gives results for Gaussian channels with a power limit.

arxiv:2611.19716.text: Set-based State Estimation for Unknown Dynamical Systems from Noisy Output Data with Probabilistic Guarantees. From Georgios Pantazis and colleagues. Estimating hidden states is difficult when system dynamics are unknown and only noisy input and output data are available. This work develops a way to bound possible states without assuming a model structure or having measured states for training. It uses a linear program to balance tight state estimates against coverage of observed outputs, with guarantees that can account for measurement noise. Simulations support the resulting probabilistic guarantees for including the true state and limiting the size of the estimated state set.

arxiv:2611.20411.text: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses. From Ruopei Fu and colleagues. Transfer learning can be difficult when source and target data use different ordered outcome categories and have different underlying models. The study develops two methods that combine source and target data, then adjust the result for the target domain. Under suitable conditions, both methods achieve optimal rates for estimating parameters and reducing prediction risk. In simulations and a medical data application, the full-target method predicts better than the sample-split method and the target-only and pooled baselines.

arxiv:2611.20115.text: Sequential Semantic-Non-Semantic Watermarking: Robustness Against UnMarker Attacks. From Md Ifraham Iqbal. Removing a watermark can threaten the ability to trace digital images, especially when attacks target different kinds of watermarks. This study tests a method that embeds both HiDDeN and StegaStamp, using fifty images and several watermark-removal attacks. Both marks remain easy to decode after embedding, and a single attack generally leaves one mark intact. Sequential attacks are needed to substantially weaken both, suggesting that layered watermarking can better resist single-stage removal.

arxiv:2611.21254.text: Dimension-free spectral laws and the risk of spectral filters. From Chen Cheng. High-dimensional spectral theory often assumes that data dimension grows in step with sample size, an assumption that does not fit functional data or kernel methods in a fixed, infinite-dimensional space. This work develops dimension-free tools for observations in a Hilbert space, giving explicit error bounds for approximating both sample covariance spectra and prediction risk. The risk results cover a wider range of analytic filters than earlier work, including iterated ridge and gradient flow. The theory also recovers the familiar proportional-dimension setting.

arxiv:2611.20976.text: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning. From Varun Agrawal and colleagues. Enterprise data often lacks the business meaning and reporting rules that artificial intelligence needs, because this knowledge is scattered across systems and people's experience. Living Context Graph builds a context layer from existing data, then learns from verified results and revises knowledge when later results contradict it. On text-to-SQL tests across three databases, learning from earlier questions improved accuracy on untouched questions by 22.6 percentage points, outperforming retrieval from the same history. The graph kept this learned context efficient to use, reducing query costs and delays.

arxiv:2611.19970.text: Physics-Informed Fractional Load Forecasting With Memory-Aware Break Detection for Reserve Scheduling. From Ali Nikseresht. Day-ahead load forecasts guide how much balancing reserve, including stored energy, power systems need. This work combines delayed building responses to temperature, shifts in demand, and persistent forecast errors in one forecasting and reserve-scheduling framework. It shows that ignoring persistent errors can lead to false break detections, and develops a detector that controls false alarms while estimating breaks and memory together. Tests in two eastern United States regions, including the pandemic period, improve forecast accuracy and sharply reduce days when storage limits are breached.

arxiv:2611.21209.text: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control. From Lucas Schulze and colleagues. Robot controllers that learn the physics of motion can struggle when payloads or other dynamics are uncertain, and noisy measurements can make their predictions sensitive to disturbances. BoBDeLaN combines a context encoder that forgets its starting state with stable filters that shape how measurement noise affects its estimates. In simulated and real robot tasks, it showed lower sensitivity to high-frequency disturbances, smaller torque prediction errors, and smoother motion than a long short-term memory encoder with the same input filter. It also degraded less when disturbances were added.

arxiv:2611.19782.text: Efficient Recursive Evaluation of Gaussian, Gamma, and Inverse Gaussian Tail Probabilities. From Joshua Joseph George and colleagues. Computing accurate tail probabilities can become costly when high-order approximations require repeated derivatives and nested sums. This work derives recursive methods for Gaussian, gamma, and inverse Gaussian tails, using a fixed number of previously computed values at each step. The methods generate approximations through order n with work that grows linearly, rather than cubically for Gaussian and gamma tails or to the fourth power for inverse Gaussian tails. Numerical results agree very well with values reported in earlier studies.

arxiv:2611.21359.text: K-out-of-N Oblivious Transfer over Erasure Channels: Capacity and Reductions. From Amirhossein Shekofteh and colleagues. Choosing several private messages from a server creates a tradeoff: the client must hide which messages it wants, while learning nothing about the rest. For binary erasure channels, the work determines the best possible rate for retrieving any chosen number of messages. It also shows that repeating a smaller one-out-of-many protocol can sometimes achieve the best rate, while repeating an optimal one-out-of-many protocol is not always optimal for retrieving several messages. The results are also extended to a generalized erasure channel.

arxiv:2611.21314.text: Reference Replay for Excitation Injection and Subsequent Exponential Convergence under Concurrent Learning Adaptive Control. From Tom Kaufmann and colleagues. Concurrent learning can identify unknown system parameters accurately, but only if the system collects sufficiently informative data during operation. This work proposes replaying a training segment in the reference signal until such data are collected, and gives an offline test to check whether the segment can provide them. It proves that the required data will appear in finite time and gives a bound on how long this can take. The analysis also shows that higher control gains can bring the data in earlier replay cycles, a result demonstrated in an academic simulation.
